WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- The House of Representatives on Tuesday passed a bill that would make suing for pay discrimination easier by altering a time limit on such suits. The act is named for Lilly Ledbetter, seen here in 2008. Her discrimination lawsuit victory was overturned in 2007. The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which passed 250-177, would give workers alleging unequal pay the right to sue within 180 days of their most recent paycheck. Current law says such employees must sue within 180 days of receiving their first unfair paycheck. Supporters of the new legislation say that, under the current law, an employer merely needs to hide unfair pay practices for three months before being able to continue them without penalty. The act, named for a former Goodyear Tire employee who sued the company for gender discrimination in 1998, would effectively overturn a 2007 Supreme Court decision on the limit. Ledbetter was awarded $360,000 in back pay by a federal judge in Alabama, but the verdict was overturned in a 5-4 Supreme Court ruling in May 2007. The court said that even though she filed her complaint within 180 days of when she first learned that she was getting paid less than comparable male employees, she had failed to file within 180 days of the first unequal paycheck. After Tuesday's House vote, Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the chamber had "taken a bold step" in passing the legislation. "In doing so, it has injected fairness, reason and common sense back into policy," Pelosi said. The legislation, which passed the Senate on Thursday, now goes to President Barack Obama, who has promised to sign it into law. It is the first major piece of legislation Congress has sent to Obama for his approval. On the campaign trail, Obama and Republican nominee Sen. John McCain debated the bill. Obama heavily emphasized what he called the plan's benefits to working women, while McCain criticized it as a boon for trial lawyers. Pelosi said Obama called to congratulate her on the bill's passage. Obama danced with Ledbetter at one of his inaugural balls, and she spoke at the Democrat National Convention at which he accepted his party's nomination. "My case is over -- I will never receive the pay I deserve," Ledbetter said in that speech. "But there will be a far richer reward if we secure fair pay for our children and grandchildren, so that no one will ever again experience the discrimination that I did."

# House Passes Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, Reversing Supreme Court Decision

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The House of Representatives approved the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act on Friday, moving to expand workers' rights to sue over wage discrimination and effectively overturning a controversial Supreme Court ruling that critics said made it harder for employees to challenge unequal pay.

The measure passed by a vote of 250 to 177, largely along party lines, with Democrats championing the bill as a critical step toward closing the gender pay gap.

## The Bill's Origins

The legislation is named for Lilly Ledbetter, a former supervisor at a Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company plant in Alabama who discovered near the end of her career that she had been paid significantly less than her male counterparts for years.

Ledbetter sued the company, and a jury initially sided with her. However, her case reached the Supreme Court, which ruled against her in 2007's *Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.*

## The Supreme Court Case It Overturns

In its 5-4 decision, the high court held that employees must file wage discrimination claims within 180 days of an employer's original decision to pay them less — even if the worker was unaware of the pay disparity at the time.

The ruling effectively barred Ledbetter's claim because the initial discriminatory pay decisions had occurred years before she learned about them.

The new legislation directly counters that interpretation, clarifying that the 180-day statute of limitations resets with each discriminatory paycheck an employee receives, rather than only at the time of the original pay decision.

## Reaction from Lawmakers

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi hailed the legislation as a landmark for workplace fairness.

"Today, this Congress will make history by sending to the president's desk a bill that says pay discrimination is unacceptable in America," Pelosi said. She emphasized that the measure would restore protections that the Supreme Court decision had stripped away, ensuring workers "have their day in court."

## The President Weighs In

President Obama, who had made equal pay a theme of his campaign, praised the bill's passage and signaled his intention to sign it into law. The measure is poised to become the first bill he signs as president.

"I look forward to signing this bill, which upholds one of this nation's founding principles: that we are all created equal and each deserve a chance to pursue our own version of happiness," Obama said in a statement.

The president called the legislation "a wonderful gift" for American workers and their families, adding that it "sends a clear message that making our economy work means making sure it works for everyone."

## What Comes Next

With the House approval following earlier Senate passage, the bill now heads to the president's desk. Supporters say the law will empower workers — particularly women and minorities — who face pay discrimination but may not immediately discover it.

Critics, largely Republicans, argued the measure could open the door to a flood of lawsuits and expose businesses to claims stemming from pay decisions made many years in the past.

Despite that opposition, Democrats celebrated the vote as a long-awaited correction to what they characterized as an unjust Supreme Court ruling.

**WASHINGTON** — Congress has passed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, landmark legislation aimed at making it easier for workers to challenge pay discrimination in the workplace. The measure was signed into law by President Barack Obama on January 29, 2009, marking the first bill he signed as president.

## Background

The legislation is named for Lilly Ledbetter, a former supervisor at a Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company plant in Gadsden, Alabama. Near the end of her nearly two-decade career, Ledbetter discovered she had been paid significantly less than her male counterparts performing the same work.

Ledbetter sued under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Though a jury initially found in her favor, the case reached the Supreme Court, which ruled against her in the 2007 decision *Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.* The Court held, in a 5-4 decision, that discrimination claims must be filed within 180 days of the original discriminatory pay decision—even if the employee was unaware of the disparity at the time.

## What the Law Does

The new law effectively reverses that Supreme Court ruling. It clarifies that the 180-day statute of limitations for filing an equal-pay lawsuit resets with each new discriminatory paycheck, rather than only at the time of the initial pay decision.

Supporters argue this addresses a fundamental problem: employees often do not know they are being paid unfairly until years after the discrimination begins, since salary information is frequently kept confidential.

## Reactions

Advocates for the law, including women's rights and labor organizations, hailed its passage as a significant victory for workplace fairness. "Making our economy work means making sure it works for everybody," President Obama said at the signing ceremony, with Ledbetter standing at his side.

Critics, largely from the business community, expressed concern that the law could expose employers to lawsuits over pay decisions made many years earlier, potentially making it difficult to defend against claims when relevant records or witnesses are no longer available.

While Ledbetter herself will not receive back pay as a result of the legislation, she has said her fight was about ensuring future workers would have stronger protections. The law is expected to have broad implications for pay discrimination cases going forward, reaffirming Congress's intent regarding the enforcement of equal-pay provisions under existing civil rights law.

# Congress Passes Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, Expanding Workers' Rights in Pay Discrimination Cases

**WASHINGTON** — Congress has passed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, landmark legislation that significantly expands the ability of workers to challenge pay discrimination, marking a major victory for equal-pay advocates.

The bill, named after Alabama resident Lilly Ledbetter, restores protections that had been narrowed by a 2007 Supreme Court decision. It became the first piece of legislation signed into law by President Barack Obama in January 2009.

## The Original Goodyear Case

The legislation stems from Ledbetter's experience as a longtime employee at a Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company plant in Gadsden, Alabama. Near the end of her nearly two-decade career, Ledbetter discovered she had been paid significantly less than her male counterparts performing the same work.

She filed a lawsuit alleging pay discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. A jury initially sided with Ledbetter, but the case ultimately reached the Supreme Court.

In *Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.* (2007), the Court ruled 5-4 against Ledbetter. The majority held that under existing law, employees must file discrimination claims within 180 days of the employer's original decision to set a discriminatory pay rate. Because Ledbetter had not filed within 180 days of that initial decision—even though she was unaware of the disparity at the time—her claim was deemed untimely.

## How the Law Changes the 180-Day Rule

The central issue in the Ledbetter case was how the 180-day statute of limitations should be calculated. The Supreme Court's ruling meant that the clock started ticking when the discriminatory pay decision was first made—a moment employees often have no way of knowing about.

The Fair Pay Act reverses this interpretation. Under the new law, the 180-day filing window resets **each time an employee receives a paycheck** affected by a discriminatory pay decision. In effect, each new paycheck that reflects the discrimination is treated as a fresh act of discrimination, restarting the statute of limitations.

This change addresses what critics of the Supreme Court decision described as a fundamental unfairness: workers frequently do not learn of pay disparities until years after they begin, often because salary information is confidential.

## Reaction and Significance

Supporters of the legislation, including women's rights and labor organizations, hailed the law as a critical tool for combating wage discrimination based on sex, race, national origin, age, religion, and disability.

Opponents, largely from the business community, warned that the law could expose employers to lawsuits over pay decisions made many years—even decades—earlier, potentially complicating record-keeping and defense against claims.

Ledbetter herself, who never recovered back pay from her own case, became a prominent advocate for the legislation, testifying before Congress and speaking publicly about her experience. Though the law did not benefit her personally, she has said her goal was to ensure future workers would not face the same barriers.

The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act remains one of the most significant recent expansions of federal anti-discrimination protections in the workplace.

# The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act: A Landmark in the Fight for Equal Pay

## Introduction

On January 29, 2009, President Barack Obama signed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act into law—the first piece of major legislation he enacted as president. The bill carried both practical and symbolic weight, addressing pay discrimination while signaling the priorities of a new administration. Behind the law stood a woman named Lilly Ledbetter, whose personal battle for equal pay reached the highest court in the land before Congress ultimately responded on her behalf.

## The Story Behind the Law

Lilly Ledbetter worked as a supervisor at a Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company plant in Gadsden, Alabama, for nearly two decades. Near the end of her career, she received an anonymous note revealing that she was being paid significantly less than her male counterparts—some of whom had less experience. Over years of employment, these disparities had compounded, affecting not only her salary but also her overtime pay and eventual retirement benefits.

Ledbetter filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and later sued Goodyear under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination based on sex, among other protected characteristics. A jury initially sided with Ledbetter, awarding her substantial damages.

## The 2007 Supreme Court Ruling

The case, *Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.*, ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court. In a 5–4 decision issued on May 29, 2007, the Court ruled against Ledbetter.

The central issue was timing. Under Title VII, employees must file a discrimination claim within 180 days of the discriminatory act. Writing for the majority, Justice Samuel Alito held that this 180-day clock began ticking when the discriminatory pay decision was originally made—not with each subsequent paycheck reflecting that decision. Because Ledbetter's pay disparities originated years earlier, the Court concluded her claim was untimely.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote a forceful dissent, which she read aloud from the bench—a rare gesture signaling strong disagreement. She argued that the majority's interpretation ignored the realities of workplace pay discrimination, which often occurs in small, hidden increments over time. Employees frequently do not know they are being underpaid because salary information is typically confidential. Ginsburg explicitly called on Congress to correct the Court's interpretation, writing that "the ball is in Congress' court."

## Congress Responds

Congress took up Ginsburg's challenge. The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act was designed to overturn the specific interpretation set forth in the Supreme Court's ruling.

The law's key provision established that the 180-day statute of limitations **resets with each discriminatory paycheck**. In other words, every new paycheck affected by a discriminatory pay decision constitutes a fresh violation, restarting the clock. This effectively restored the interpretation of the law that many courts had applied before the *Ledbetter* decision.

Importantly, the act did not create new categories of rights or change the fundamental protections of Title VII. Instead, it clarified when the filing period begins, ensuring that workers who discover long-standing pay discrimination are not barred from seeking justice simply because the original decision occurred years earlier.

## Significance as Obama's First Major Bill

That the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act became the first major bill Obama signed carried considerable significance:

**A statement of priorities.** By choosing this legislation as his first, Obama signaled that civil rights, workplace fairness, and gender equity would be central themes of his presidency.

**Symbolic power.** The signing ceremony featured Lilly Ledbetter herself, transforming an ordinary worker's struggle into a national symbol. Ledbetter never recovered her own lost wages—the law was not retroactive to her case—but she became an advocate for others facing similar circumstances.

**A response to judicial interpretation.** The law demonstrated the constitutional dynamic between the branches of government. When the Supreme Court interpreted a statute in a way Congress found contrary to its intent, the legislative branch responded by amending the law—exactly the process Justice Ginsburg had invited.

**Momentum for equal pay advocacy.** The act reinvigorated discussions about the persistent gender pay gap and paved the way for continued debate over additional measures, such as the proposed Paycheck Fairness Act.

## Conclusion

The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act stands as a notable example of how personal struggle, judicial decision-making, and legislative action can intersect. Though the Supreme Court's 2007 ruling closed the courthouse doors on Lilly Ledbetter's individual claim, her name became attached to a law that reopened them for countless others. As the first major bill of the Obama administration, it also underscored the enduring national conversation about fairness, equality, and the ongoing pursuit of equal pay for equal work.
